cap: The vaginal wall is built to stretch and to stay acid, not to secrete. Elastic lamina propria and smooth muscle let it distend, glycogen-rich nonkeratinized epithelium feeds the lactobacilli that make lactic acid, and with no glands of its own, lubrication arrives as a plasma transudate plus mucus from the vestibular glands. A blocked Bartholin duct, lined by transitional epithelium, makes the cyst or abscess at 4 or 8 o'clock; Skene gland infection causes urethral symptoms; a Gartner duct cyst sits higher on the lateral wall.
teach: Read the left panel from the surface inward: each layer answers one need. The epithelium resists friction and stores glycogen, the lamina propria supplies elasticity and the vascular plexus that produces the transudate, the muscle follows the stretch, and the adventitia anchors the canal. Because no layer holds glands, every secretion must come from outside the wall: cervical mucus from above, and vestibular gland mucus from below. The right panel shows where those lower glands open. Bartholin glands sit at the posterolateral vestibule, which is why a cyst bulges there; a Gartner cyst arises from a wolffian remnant and lies on the vaginal wall itself.
